name: Uniform circle formation

origin.note: The first deterministic solution (SSS 2006); circle formation with convergence towards uniformity predates it [Defago2002Circle].

derived_from.relation: Uniform circle formation is "an important special case of the geometric pattern formation problem" [Feletti2024Optimal]: the target is the regular $n$-gon. It is also the special case of circle formation with equal spacing; circle formation is "its precursor" [Feletti2024Optimal].

related.relation: A uniform circle is a circle, so every uniform-circle algorithm forms a circle.

summary: Robots must form a regular $n$-gon: a circle with equal spacing.
statement: $n$ robots start at distinct points and must reach the vertices of a regular $n$-gon (in any position and size) and stay there. **Time** is in epochs (ASYNC: intervals in which every robot completes at least one full Look–Compute–Move cycle) or rounds; **colours** count light colours in the luminous model.

primer.intro: Picture guards who must stand evenly spaced around a circular fence that nobody has built: the circle and the spacing must come from the guards themselves. There are $n$ **robots**, points at distinct places in the plane; their positions form the **configuration**. Each robot repeats a **Look–Compute–Move cycle**: it takes a **snapshot** of where the other robots are (Look), decides on a destination point (Compute) and moves towards it (Move). They are identical, silent, **oblivious** (no memory between cycles), and each uses its own **local coordinate system**, so they agree on no direction and no handedness. The **scheduler** (an adversary) decides the **activation** of robots, that is, when each performs a cycle, and is ASYNC: each phase may take any finite time. Every move is a **non-rigid move**: a robot may be stopped after a minimum distance $\delta$. The robots must reach the **vertices** of a **regular $n$-gon** (a polygon with $n$ equal sides and equal angles), one robot on each vertex, of any size and position, and stay there.

ideas.title: Fix the smallest enclosing circle, reach it, then let symmetric robots move as one
ideas.idea:
1. Compute the **smallest enclosing circle** (SEC) of all robots; every robot computes the same circle. All moves are chosen so that this circle does not change.
2. Robots inside the circle move out to it, as in circle formation.
3. With all robots on the circle, group them into **analogy classes**: two robots are analogous if some symmetry of the whole configuration maps one to the other.
4. The scheduler could make analogous robots act identically anyway, so the algorithm makes each class always move together, deliberately and symmetrically.
5. The robots compute the vertices of a regular $n$-gon on the circle and move to them class by class. Special configurations that are already close to regular (pre-regular, biangular) get their own procedure.
ideas.analysis: The overall plan is simple; the difficulty is that asynchronous robots act on outdated snapshots, so the analogy classes and destinations that one robot computes may already be stale. Flocchini, Prencipe, Santoro and Viglietta show that oblivious, disoriented robots with non-rigid moves form a regular $n$-gon in ASYNC from every initial configuration at distinct points, for every $n$ [Flocchini2017Uniform]; the case $n = 4$ is solved in [Mamino2016Square]. Time is not analysed; for opaque robots with lights, $O(1)$ epochs and $O(1)$ colours suffice [Feletti2024Optimal].
ideas.why_it_matters: It closed a long-standing question and showed that, for pattern formation, asynchrony, chirality and rigid moves do not add computational power.

ideas.title: Two robots on the same point can never be separated
ideas.idea: Suppose two robots start at the same point. They get exactly the same snapshot. The adversary gives them identical local coordinate systems and the scheduler always activates them together. Identical robots with identical snapshots and identical local coordinate systems compute the same destination, so they move together and are still on one point after every cycle. A regular $n$-gon has $n$ distinct vertices, so it is never formed.
ideas.analysis: This is why the problem asks for distinct starting points; Flocchini et al. note that with two robots on one point the problem is \"easily seen to be unsolvable\" [Flocchini2017Uniform]. The same trap is the reason careful algorithms never let two robots meet while they move.
ideas.why_it_matters: It is the simplest example of a symmetry that oblivious deterministic robots can never break.

ideas.title: Why only the point and the regular polygon can be formed from every initial configuration
ideas.idea: Start the robots on a regular $n$-gon. Give every robot a local coordinate system whose $x$-axis points to the centre, all with the same unit. All robots get the same snapshot; if the scheduler activates all of them together, they all make the same move up to rotation, so the configuration stays a regular $n$-gon (or collapses to its centre). So from this initial configuration the only formable patterns are the regular $n$-gon and the single point.
ideas.analysis: Suzuki and Yamashita showed that the patterns formable from an initial configuration depend on its **symmetricity**, its amount of rotational symmetry [Suzuki1999Formation]; the regular $n$-gon has the most. Hence the point (gathering) and the regular $n$-gon (uniform circle) are the only patterns that might be formable from every initial configuration, and both are [Flocchini2017Uniform].
ideas.why_it_matters: It explains why the uniform circle is singled out among all patterns: it is one of only two universally formable ones.

glossary.definition: a computing entity modelled as a point of the plane (a unit disc for fat robots); all robots run the same algorithm
the positions of all $n$ robots at one instant, a multiset of points of the plane

one activation of a robot: in Look it takes a snapshot, in Compute it determines a destination point from that snapshot alone (and its own light, where lights exist), in Move it travels towards that point
the configuration as a robot observes it in Look (with the colours of the lights it sees, where lights exist), expressed in its local coordinate system
a robot keeps no memory from one Look–Compute–Move cycle to the next: Compute uses only the current snapshot

the origin, axes, unit of length and handedness in which a robot expresses its snapshot and its destination; robots agree on none of these unless the setting assumes chirality, one common axis or a common compass

the adversary that decides when each robot is activated: FSYNC activates every robot in every round, SSYNC a nonempty subset of the robots in each round, the sequential scheduler exactly one robot per round, and ASYNC lets each phase of each cycle take any finite time; every robot is activated infinitely often
the scheduler's choice to let a robot perform one Look–Compute–Move cycle; a robot that is not activated stays still
a move that the adversary may stop before the destination, but only after the robot has travelled at least the distance $\delta$
an interval of an ASYNC execution in which every robot completes at least one full Look–Compute–Move cycle; a bound of $X$ epochs holds for every division of the execution into consecutive epochs
a polygon with $n$ vertices, equal sides and equal angles; here of any position and size
one of the $n$ corner points of the regular $n$-gon, each to be occupied by one robot
the unique smallest circle that contains a given finite set of points (by default the robots of the configuration), abbreviated SEC; it does not depend on any local coordinate system
a set of robots that the symmetries of the whole configuration map onto one another; two robots in one class are analogous

history: Uniform circle formation was first asked as **solvability**: can disoriented oblivious robots form a regular polygon? It was solved for SSYNC [Dieudonne2008Circle] and then for ASYNC without chirality or rigidity [Flocchini2017Uniform] [Mamino2016Square]. Only after feasibility was settled did the community turn to **time and colours** for luminous opaque robots [Feletti2023Schedulers] [Pattanayak2024TimeColor], reaching $O(1)$ epochs with $O(1)$ colours [Feletti2024Optimal].

measures.name: Time
measures.description: rounds (FSYNC, SSYNC) or epochs (ASYNC) until the task is done; "finite" when only solvability is known

measures.name: Colours
measures.description: colours of the light per robot (0 for oblivious robots)

variants.title: ASYNC, oblivious, disoriented
variants.summary: Oblivious, disoriented, non-rigid robots form a regular $n$-gon from any configuration of distinct points, for every $n$.

preconditions: if two robots start at the same point

results.note: Introductory for ASYNC and current best. The case $n = 4$ (square formation) is solved by [Mamino2016Square].
Completes the picture: synchrony, chirality and rigidity are computationally irrelevant for pattern formation.

time.note: No time analysis of oblivious ASYNC uniform circle formation is recorded.

open: Can oblivious robots without lights form a uniform circle in $O(1)$ epochs, with rigid or non-rigid moves? [Feletti2024Optimal]
variants.notes: Uniform circle and point are the only patterns formable from every initial configuration [Flocchini2017Uniform].

variants.title: SSYNC, oblivious
variants.summary: The first deterministic uniform circle formation, for $n \ge 5$ semi-synchronous robots.
variants.notes: Dieudonné and Petit later solved $n \ne 4$ and $n = 4$ in SSYNC (SIROCCO 2007, ISAAC 2008; not yet in the bibliography).

variants.title: Opaque robots with lights, ASYNC
variants.summary: With lights, opaque robots form a uniform circle in $O(1)$ epochs with $O(1)$ colours, which is optimal in both.

results.note: First ASYNC result for opaque luminous robots (ICTCS 2022; journal 2023); $O(1)$ time in FSYNC and SSYNC.
A time–colour trade-off for $x \in [1, O(\log\log n)]$: $O(1)$ time with $O(\sqrt n)$ colours, or $O(\log\log n)$ time with $O(1)$ colours. Abstract only.
Asymptotically optimal in time and colours.

colours.note: $\Theta(1)$ colours; the exact minimum is open.

open: What is the exact minimum number of colours for $O(1)$-epoch uniform circle formation in ASYNC? [Feletti2024Optimal]
Uniform circle formation with non-rigid moves in the luminous opaque model [Feletti2024Optimal].
variants.notes: Robots are punctiform, disoriented and do not know $n$; collisions are avoided. The only lower bounds are trivial. Checked against the full texts of [Feletti2023Log] and [Feletti2024Optimal].

variants.title: Opaque robots with lights, FSYNC
variants.summary: In FSYNC, opaque luminous robots form a uniform circle in 3 cycles with $O(1)$ colours.

results.note: First paper on the opaque luminous model; as described by [Feletti2024Optimal].

variants.notes: In SSYNC the same paper takes $O(1)$ rounds. The ICTCS 2022 version was read in full.

variants.title: Transparent fat robots, SSYNC
variants.summary: Transparent fat robots that agree on one axis form a regular $n$-gon of given side in SSYNC.

assumes: $n$ and the side length are known
only the direction of the $y$ axis is shared, without chirality
results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 1). A preprint.

variants.notes: The paper assumes agreement on one axis without chirality, which is the catalogue's one-axis value. Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Opaque fat robots, ASYNC, limited visibility, compass
variants.summary: Opaque fat robots with limited visibility and a common coordinate system form a uniform circle of given centre and radius in ASYNC.

assumes: the circle's centre and radius are given
results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 1). A preprint.

figure.caption: Uniform circle formation: $n$ oblivious robots at distinct points must occupy the vertices of a regular $n$-gon, of any position and size, and stay there [Flocchini2017Uniform]. Shown in SSYNC rounds (ringed robots are activated), simplified from [Flocchini2017Uniform]: the smallest enclosing circle (dashed) never changes; robots inside move out to it, then robots on it move to the vertices of a regular hexagon inscribed in it (hollow).
